danish.title: Ottende bog (1811–12) — Kapitel 5
paragraphs: Boris var det ikke lykkedes at gøre et rigt parti i Petersborg, så med det samme formål for øje var han kommet til Moskva. Der vaklede han mellem de to rigeste arvinger, Julie og fyrstinde Marja. Selvom fyrstinde Marja trods sin mangel på skønhed forekom ham mere tiltrækkende end Julie, følte han af en eller anden grund, han ikke kunne forklare, sig akavet ved at gøre kur til hende. Ved deres seneste møde på den gamle fyrstes navnedag havde hun besvaret alle hans forsøg på at tale sentimentalt helt tilfældigt og tydeligvis uden at lytte til, hvad han sagde.
Julie derimod modtog hans opmærksomheder gerne, om end på sin egen særegne måde.

Hun var syvogtyve. Efter sine brødres død var hun blevet meget velhavende. Hun var nu afgjort uskøn, men troede sig ikke blot lige så smuk som før, men endda langt mere tiltrækkende. Hun blev bestyrket i denne indbildning af, at hun var blevet en meget rig arving, og af at jo ældre hun blev, des mindre farlig blev hun for mænd, og des friere kunne de omgås hende og nyde hendes soupeer, soiréer og det livlige selskab, der samledes i hendes hus, uden at påtage sig nogen forpligtelse. En mand, der ti år tidligere ville have frygtet at komme hver dag i et hus, hvor der var en pige på sytten, af frygt for at kompromittere hende og binde sig, kom nu dristigt hver dag og behandlede hende ikke som en ung kvinde, man kunne gifte sig med, men som en kønsløs bekendt.

Den vinter var Karaginernes hus det mest behagelige og gæstfrie i Moskva. Foruden de formelle aften- og middagsselskaber samledes hver dag et stort selskab, hovedsagelig af mænd, som spiste souper ved midnat og blev til klokken tre om morgenen. Julie forsømte aldrig et bal, en promenade eller en forestilling. Hendes kjoler var altid af den nyeste mode. Men trods dette virkede hun desillusioneret over alt og fortalte alle, at hun hverken troede på venskab eller kærlighed, eller nogen af livets glæder, og at hun kun ventede sig fred »hist henne«. Hun antog tonen hos en, der har lidt en stor skuffelse, som en pige der enten har mistet den mand, hun elskede, eller er blevet grusomt bedraget af ham. Selvom intet sådant var hændt hende, blev hun betragtet i det lys, og havde endda selv overbevist sig om, at hun havde lidt meget i livet. Denne melankoli, der ikke forhindrede hende i at more sig, hindrede ikke de unge mennesker, der kom i hendes hus, i at tilbringe tiden behageligt. Enhver gæst ydede sin tribut til værtindens melankolske stemning og morede sig så med selskabssladder, dans, intellektuelle lege og bouts rimés, der var på mode hos Karaginerne. Kun nogle få af de unge mænd, heriblandt Boris, gik dybere ind i Julies melankoli, og med dem førte hun langvarige private samtaler om alle jordiske tings forfængelighed, og for dem viste hun sit album fuldt af sørgelige skitser, sentenser og vers.

Over for Boris var Julie særlig nådig: hun beklagede hans tidlige desillusion med livet, tilbød ham den trøst fra venskab, som hun, der selv havde lidt så meget, kunne yde, og viste ham sit album. Boris tegnede to træer i albummet og skrev: »Landlige træer, jeres mørke grene spreder trøstesløshed og vemod over mig.«
På en anden side tegnede han en grav og skrev:
La mort est secourable et la mort est tranquille. Ah! contre les douleurs il n'y a pas d'autre asile.*
* Døden giver lindring og døden er fredelig. Ak! mod lidelser er der ingen anden tilflugt.
Julie sagde, det var henrivende.

»Der er noget så fortryllende i melankoliens smil,« sagde hun til Boris, idet hun ord for ord gentog en passage, hun havde kopieret fra en bog. »Det er en lysstråle i mørket, en skygge mellem tristhed og fortvivlelse, der viser muligheden for trøst.«
Som svar skrev Boris disse linjer:

Aliment de poison d'une âme trop sensible, Toi, sans qui le bonheur me serait impossible, Tendre mélancholie, ah, viens me consoler, Viens calmer les tourments de ma sombre retraite, Et mêle une douceur secrète A ces pleurs que je sens couler.*

* Giftig næring for en alt for følsom sjæl, du, uden hvem jeg aldrig kunne kende lykken! Ømme tungsind, kom og trøst mig, stil kvalen i min mørke ensomhed, og bland en hemmelig sødme i de tårer, jeg mærker rinde.

For Boris spillede Julie de mest sørgmodige nokturner på sin harpe. Boris læste Stakkels Lisa højt for hende og afbrød mere end én gang oplæsningen, fordi de følelser, der kvalte ham. Når de mødtes til store sammenkomster, så Julie og Boris hinanden som de eneste sjæle, der forstod hinanden i en verden af ligegyldige mennesker.

Anna Mikhajlovna, der ofte besøgte Karaginerne, forhørte sig omhyggeligt, mens hun spillede kort med moderen, om Julies medgift (hun skulle have to godser i Penza og skovene i Nizjnij Novgorod). Anna Mikhajlovna betragtede den forfinede tristhed, der forenede hendes søn med den velhavende Julie, med rørelse og hengivenhed til Guds vilje.

»Du er altid charmerende og melankolsk, kære Julie,« sagde hun til datteren. »Boris siger, at hans sjæl finder ro i dit hus. Han har lidt så mange skuffelser og er så følsom,« sagde hun til moderen. »Ak, min kære, jeg kan ikke fortælle Dem, hvor glad jeg er blevet for Julie i den sidste tid,« sagde hun til sin søn. »Men hvem kan lade være med at elske hende? Hun er et englevæsen! Ak, Boris, Boris!« — hun holdt inde. »Og hvor medynk jeg har med hendes mor,« fortsatte hun; »i dag viste hun mig sine regnskaber og breve fra Penza (de har enorme godser dér), og hun, stakkel, har ingen til at hjælpe sig, og de snyder hende så!«

Boris smilede næppe mærkbart, mens han lyttede til sin mor. Han lo mildt ad hendes naive diplomati, men lyttede til hvad hun havde at sige, og spurgte somme tider omhyggeligt ind til godserne i Penza og Nizjnij Novgorod.

Julie havde længe ventet et frieri fra sin melankolske tilbeder og var parat til at sige ja; men en hemmelig følelse af afsky for hende, for hendes lidenskabelige ønske om at blive gift, for hendes kunstlighed, og en følelse af rædsel ved at give afkald på muligheden for ægte kærlighed holdt stadig Boris tilbage. Hans orlov nærmede sig sin afslutning. Han tilbragte hver dag og hele dage hos Karaginerne, og hver dag, når han tænkte sagen igennem, sagde han til sig selv, at han ville fri i morgen. Men i Julies selskab, når han betragtede hendes røde ansigt og hage (næsten altid pudret), hendes fugtige øjne og hendes udtryk af stadig parathed til øjeblikkeligt at skifte fra melankoli til en unaturlig henrykkelse over ægteskabelig lykke, kunne Boris ikke frembringe de afgørende ord, selvom han i fantasien længe havde betragtet sig som ejer af Penza-godserne og skovene i Nizjnij Novgorod og allokeret brugen af indtægterne derfra. Julie så Boris' ubeslutsomhed, og somme tider faldt det hende ind, at hun var frastødende for ham, men hendes kvindelige selvbedrag forsynede hende straks med trøst, og hun sagde til sig selv, at han kun var genert af kærlighed. Hendes melankoli begyndte imidlertid at slå over i pirrelighed, og ikke længe før Boris' afrejse lagde hun en bestemt plan. Netop da Boris' orlov var ved at udløbe, dukkede Anatol Kuragin op i Moskva, og naturligvis i Karaginernes salon, og Julie opgav pludselig sin melankoli, blev munter og meget opmærksom på Kuragin.

»Min kære,« sagde Anna Mikhajlovna til sin søn, »jeg ved fra en pålidelig kilde, at fyrst Vasilij har sendt sin søn til Moskva for at få ham gift med Julie. Jeg er så glad for Julie, at det ville gøre mig ondt. Hvad mener du, min kære?«

Tanken om at blive til grin og om at have smidt hele den måned med besværlig melankolsk tjeneste hos Julie ud, og om at se alle indtægterne fra Penza-godserne, som han allerede mentalt havde fordelt og sat til passende brug, falde i hænderne på en anden, og især i hænderne på den idiot Anatol, smerter Boris. Han kørte til Karaginerne med den faste hensigt at fri. Julie modtog ham i en munter, ubekymret tone, talte uforpligtende om, hvor morsomt hun havde haft det til gårsdagens bal, og spurgte, hvornår han rejste. Selvom Boris var kommet med den bestemte hensigt at tale om sin kærlighed og derfor ville være øm, begyndte han irriteret at tale om kvindelig ubestandighed, om hvor let kvinder kan skifte fra tristhed til glæde, og hvordan deres stemninger alene afhænger af, hvem der tilfældigvis gør kur til dem. Julie blev fornærmet og svarede, at det var sandt, at en kvinde har brug for afveksling, og at det samme om igen ville kede hvem som helst.

»Så ville jeg råde Dem...« begyndte Boris, idet han ville stikke til hende; men i det øjeblik faldt den ærgerlige tanke ham ind, at han måtte forlade Moskva uden at have nået sit mål, og have spildt sine anstrengelser forgæves — noget han aldrig tillod at ske.
Han standsede midt i sætningen, sænkede øjnene for ikke at se hendes ubehageligt irriterede og ubeslutsomme ansigt og sagde:
»Jeg er slet ikke kommet her for at skændes med Dem. Tværtimod...«

Han kiggede på hende for at sikre sig, at han kunne fortsætte. Hendes pirrelighed var pludselig helt forsvundet, og hendes urolige, bønfaldende øjne var rettet mod ham med grådig forventning. »Jeg kan altid arrangere det, så jeg ikke ser hende så tit,« tænkte Boris. »Sagen er begyndt og må fuldføres!« Han rødmede kraftigt, løftede øjnene mod hendes og sagde:
»De kender mine følelser for Dem!«

Der var ikke behov for at sige mere: Julies ansigt strålede af triumf og selvtilfredshed; men hun tvang Boris til at sige alt det, der siges ved sådanne lejligheder — at han elskede hende og aldrig havde elsket nogen anden kvinde højere. Hun vidste, at hun for Penza-godserne og skovene i Nizjnij Novgorod kunne forlange dette, og hun fik hvad hun forlangte.

Det forlovede par hentydede ikke længere til træer, der spredte trøstesløshed og vemod over dem, men planlagde indretningen af et pragtfuldt hus i Petersborg, aflagde visitter og forberedte alt til et strålende bryllup.

english.title: Book Eight (1811 - 12) — Chapter 5
paragraphs: Boris had not succeeded in making a wealthy match in Petersburg, so with the same goal in mind he came to Moscow. There he wavered between the two richest heiresses, Julie and Princess Mary. Though Princess Mary, despite her plainness, seemed more attractive to him than Julie, he felt awkward about courting her without knowing why. When they had last met on the old prince's name day, she had answered at random all his attempts at sentimental conversation, clearly not listening to what he was saying.
Julie, on the other hand, accepted his attentions readily, though in her own particular way.

She was twenty-seven. After the death of her brothers she had become very wealthy. She was by now decidedly plain, but thought herself not merely as good-looking as before but even far more attractive. She was confirmed in this delusion both by the fact that she had become a very wealthy heiress, and because the older she grew the less dangerous she became to men, and the more freely they could associate with her and take advantage of her suppers, parties, and the lively company that assembled at her house, without incurring any obligation. A man who ten years before would have been afraid of visiting daily where there was a seventeen-year-old girl, for fear of compromising her and committing himself, would now go boldly every day and treat her not as a marriageable girl but as a genderless acquaintance.

That winter the Kargins' house was the most pleasant and hospitable in Moscow. In addition to the formal evening and dinner parties, a large company, chiefly of men, gathered there every day, eating supper at midnight and staying till three in the morning. Julie never missed a ball, a promenade, or a play. Her dresses were always of the latest fashion. But despite all that, she seemed disillusioned about everything and told everyone that she didn't believe in friendship or love or any of the joys of life, and expected peace only "over there." She adopted the tone of one who has suffered a great disappointment, like a girl who has either lost the man she loved or been cruelly deceived by him. Though nothing of the kind had happened to her, she was regarded in that light, and had even herself come to believe that she had suffered much in life. This melancholy, which didn't prevent her from enjoying herself, didn't stop the young people who came to her house from having a good time. Every visitor paid tribute to the melancholy mood of their hostess, and then amused himself with society gossip, dancing, intellectual games, and rhyming games that were in fashion at the Kargins'. Only a few of these young men, among them Boris, entered more deeply into Julie's melancholy, and with these she had long private conversations about the vanity of all worldly things, and she showed them her albums filled with mournful sketches, maxims, and verses.

To Boris, Julie was especially gracious: she sympathized with his early disillusionment with life, offered him whatever consolation of friendship she — who had herself suffered so much — could give, and showed him her album. Boris sketched two trees in the album and wrote: "Rustic trees, your dark branches shed gloom and melancholy upon me."
On another page he drew a tomb, and wrote:
La mort est secourable et la mort est tranquille. Ah! contre les douleurs il n’y a pas d’autre asile. *
* Death gives relief and death is peaceful. Ah! From suffering there is no other refuge.
Julie said this was charming.

"There is something so enchanting in the smile of melancholy," she said to Boris, repeating word for word a passage she had copied from a book. "It is a ray of light in the darkness, a shade between sadness and despair, showing the possibility of consolation."
In reply Boris wrote these lines:

Aliment de poison d’une âme trop sensible, Toi, sans qui le bonheur me serait impossible, Tendre mélancholie, ah, viens me consoler, Viens calmer les tourments de ma sombre retraite, Et mêle une douceur secrète A ces pleurs que je sens couler. *

* Poisonous nourishment of a too sensitive soul, Thou, without whom happiness would be impossible for me, Tender melancholy, ah, come and console me, Come calm the torments of my gloomy retreat, And mingle a secret sweetness with these tears that I feel flowing.

For Boris, Julie played the most mournful nocturnes on her harp. Boris read Poor Liza aloud to her, and more than once interrupted the reading because of the emotions that choked him. At large gatherings, Julie and Boris looked at each other as the only souls who understood one another in a world of indifferent people.

Anna Mikhaylovna, who often visited the Kargins, would play cards with the mother while carefully inquiring about Julie's dowry — she was to have two estates in Penza and the Nizhegorod forests. Anna Mikhaylovna regarded the refined sadness that united her son to the wealthy Julie with emotion and resignation to the Divine will.

"You are always charming and melancholy, my dear Julie," she said to the daughter. "Boris says his soul finds peace at your house. He has suffered so many disappointments and is so sensitive," said she to the mother. "Oh, my dear, I can't tell you how fond I've grown of Julie lately," she said to her son. "But who could help loving her? She is an angelic being! Oh, Boris, Boris!" — she paused. "And how I pity her mother," she went on; "today she showed me her accounts and letters from Penza (they have enormous estates there), and she, poor thing, has no one to help her, and they cheat her so!"

Boris smiled almost invisibly while listening to his mother. He laughed mildly at her naive scheming but listened to what she had to say, and sometimes questioned her carefully about the Penza and Nizhegorod estates.

Julie had long been expecting a proposal from her melancholy admirer and was ready to accept it; but some secret feeling of repulsion toward her, toward her desperate desire to get married, toward her artificiality, and a feeling of horror at giving up the possibility of real love, still held Boris back. His leave was running out. He spent every day and whole days at the Kargins', and every day on thinking it over told himself that he would propose tomorrow. But in Julie's presence, looking at her red face and chin (nearly always powdered), her moist eyes, and her expression of constant readiness to switch at once from melancholy to unnatural rapture at the prospect of married bliss, Boris could not bring himself to say the decisive words, though in his imagination he had long considered himself the owner of those Penza and Nizhegorod estates and had planned how to use the income from them. Julie saw Boris's indecision, and sometimes it occurred to her that she was repulsive to him, but her feminine self-deception immediately provided consolation, and she told herself that he was only shy from love. Her melancholy, however, began to turn into irritability, and not long before Boris's departure she formed a definite plan of action. Just as Boris's leave was running out, Anatole Kuragin appeared in Moscow, and naturally in the Kargins' drawing room, and Julie, suddenly dropping her melancholy, became cheerful and very attentive to Kuragin.

"My dear," said Anna Mikhaylovna to her son, "I know from a reliable source that Prince Vasili has sent his son to Moscow to get him married to Julie. I'm so fond of Julie that I'd be sorry for her. What do you think of it, my dear?"

The idea of being made a fool of and of having thrown away that whole month of painful melancholy service to Julie, and of seeing all the revenue from the Penza estates — which he had already mentally allocated and put to proper use — fall into the hands of another, and especially into the hands of that idiot Anatole, stung Boris. He drove to the Kargins' with the firm intention of proposing. Julie met him in a gay, careless manner, spoke casually of how she had enjoyed yesterday's ball, and asked when he was leaving. Though Boris had come intentionally to speak of his love and therefore meant to be tender, he began speaking irritably about how easily women can switch from sadness to joy, and how their moods depend solely on who happens to be paying court to them. Julie was offended and replied that it was true that a woman needs variety, and the same thing over and over again would bore anyone.

"Then I should advise you..." Boris began, wanting to sting her; but at that instant the galling thought occurred to him that he might have to leave Moscow without having achieved his aim, and have wasted his efforts for nothing — which was something he never allowed to happen.
He stopped himself in the middle of the sentence, lowered his eyes to avoid seeing her unpleasantly irritated and uncertain face, and said:
"I didn't come here to quarrel with you. On the contrary..."

He glanced at her to make sure he could go on. Her irritability had suddenly vanished, and her anxious, pleading eyes were fixed on him with greedy expectation. "I can always arrange not to see her often," thought Boris. "The thing has been started and must be finished!" He blushed deeply, raised his eyes to hers, and said:
"You know my feelings for you!"

There was no need to say more: Julie's face shone with triumph and self-satisfaction; but she forced Boris to say everything that's said on such occasions — that he loved her and had never loved any other woman more than her. She knew that for the Penza estates and Nizhegorod forests she could demand this, and she received what she demanded.

The engaged couple, no longer speaking of trees that shed gloom and melancholy upon them, planned the arrangements for a splendid house in Petersburg, paid visits, and prepared everything for a brilliant wedding.
